segments.text:
`collect` calls this function at line 289 and stores the result in `D['mod']`. No rate is read here. FACTS.md uses two values as proof of 12 modules: MemTotal and the DIMM sockets message. This function reads what a boot with 10 modules shows: its DIMM sockets message and the memory size line of its Linux kernel log.
- It first reads `h-1.txt`, the saved journal of a boot of 2026-11-17 with 10 memory modules.
- `h1_start`: the start time of that boot, from the first 19 characters of line 1.
- `h1_dimm`: the number in the message `This system has N DIMM sockets` of line 2. It is 10 in this file.
segments.heading: Function `open_mod`: files that support the count of 12 modules

segments.text:
Reads two saved Linux kernel logs: `k-1.txt` of the same 10-module boot and `k-5.txt` of the boot that started on 2026-11-09.
- Each file must hold exactly one line with the text `kernel: Memory: ` in the form `...K/...K available`. If not, the `assert` stops the script.
- Example, line 762 of `k-1.txt`: `Memory: 329221340K/334981392K available`.
- `out['k-1']` and `out['k-5']` keep the line number, the two numbers (`avail_K`, `total_K`) and the first 15 characters of the line, which are its time stamp.
- `facts_text.py` stops the script unless the two `total_K` values differ by 64 x 1024 x 1024 K. FACTS.md states that the DIMM report reads this difference as 64 GiB (1 GiB = 2^30 bytes), the size of two modules.

Reads `dmi17-7200.txt`, the module list that was saved in the boot of the rerun. The file is the output of the command `dmidecode -t 17`, which prints the hardware table of the firmware. The function counts lines. For the first four counts it compares the line without the tabs and spaces at its two ends.
- `devices`: lines equal to `Memory Device`. The file holds one such entry per memory module.
- `speed`: lines equal to `Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`.
- `size`: lines equal to `Size: 32 GB`. `volatile`: lines equal to `Volatile Size: 32 GB`.
- `size_any`: lines that hold the text `Size: 32 GB` at any place. This count includes the lines of `size` and of `volatile`.
- In this file the five counts are 12, 12, 12, 12 and 24.
- `mtime`: the time of the last change of the file, in UTC, in whole seconds. `facts_text.py` stops the script unless this time lies inside the time span of row 0 of `boots.txt`. Row 0 is the boot of the rerun.

Reads `try6.txt` once more and looks for lines that start with `modules=`. Exactly one such line must exist, and it must have the form `modules=N`. If not, the `assert` stops the script.
- `try6_modules` is N, and `try6_modules_line` is the line number. In this file line 6 reads `modules=24`.
- `facts_text.py` stops the script unless N equals `size_any`, the count of the lines with the text `Size: 32 GB`.
- The module count of the records (12) does not come from this line. `collect` takes it from the DIMM sockets line of the same file, in line 56 of this script.

`collect` calls this function at line 195 with the folder `R/kernels-20261113T181222Z`, the folder of baseline A-1. The result is stored in `D['probe13']`. No rate is read here.
- The function first reads `probe.txt` of that folder.
- Every line that consists of 64 hexadecimal digits, two spaces and a name gives one entry of `sha` (name to sha256) and one entry of `sha_line` (name to line number).
- In this file the lines 18, 19 and 20 hold the values of `run_kernels.sh`, `bw_old` and `bw_new`. The checks `sha-bw` and `A-args` use them.
- No check of this script uses the entries of the source files. Line 15 records the sha256 `c1406e02...` for `bandwidth.c`. The local `bandwidth.c` in the folder `kernels-2026-11-13` has another sha256, `f1985072...`. That is the value in `probe.txt` of the run of 18:32:18 UTC on the same day, which built the binaries and timed nothing.
- Both records give the same sha256 for the binary `bw_new` (`fd7c14df...`). So the machine code is not in doubt. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text. The record of the Claude Code session of that day holds the edit (`/home/jhan/.claude/projects/-home-jhan-workspace-titan-cache-perf-crb/7663f0d2-7d09-4571-b80c-92526358fa86.jsonl`, line 1000). With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.
- `T` turns a time text such as `2026-11-13T18:12:22Z` into a date and time.
segments.heading: Function `open_probe13`: records of the first test of 2026-11-13

segments.text:
Finds three lines of the same `probe.txt` that start with `##`.
- The `## host=` line gives the start time (`utc`), the three load averages (`load_before`) and the number of logins.
- The `## one-thread done` line gives the 1-minute load average and the time at the end of the one-thread phase (`one_done_load`, `one_done_utc`).
- The `## load_after=` line gives the 1-minute load average and the time after the 120-thread part (`load_after`, `utc_after`).
- `has_memtotal` and `has_boot_id` say whether any line of the file holds the text `MemTotal` or `boot_id`. Both are false for this file. `facts_text.py` stops the script if one of them is true.

Reads `one-thread.csv` of the same folder, the result file of the one-thread phase. Only the header lines that start with `-- binary` are kept.
- `one_n` is their number (192 in this file).
- `one_first` and `one_last` are the times of day of the first and the last header line.
- No interval row of this file is used. So no one-thread rate enters the records.

Reads `h-5.txt`, the saved journal of the boot that started on 2026-11-09. The test of 2026-11-13 ran in that boot.
- `boot_start`: the start time of the boot, from line 1. `boot_dimm`: the number in the DIMM sockets message of line 2 (12 in this file).
- `first_record_line`, `first_record_utc`: the line number and the time of the first line with the text `[Hardware Error]`.
- `records_in_120`: the number of lines of the day of the test that hold `[Hardware Error]` and whose time lies from `one_done_utc` to `utc_after`, both ends included. This span is the 120-thread part of baseline A-1.
- The code counts lines here, and one record has several such lines. The count is 0 in this data.

`fd.read_error_records` returns every hardware error record of the same journal, one per line `Hardware error from APEI ...` (321 records in this file). `fd.step_headers` returns the `-- step` header lines of `A1.csv`, `A2.csv` and `A3.csv` in `R/partA-20261113T205055Z`. Each process has one such header line. The line gives the launch time of the process.
- `a2_window`: from the launch of the first process of `A1.csv` to the launch of the first process of `A2.csv`. This is the time span of baseline A-2.
- `a2_first`: the header line of the first process of `A1.csv`. `a2_csv2`: the path of `A2.csv`.

Finds the process that ran directly before the first process of baseline A-3.
- Line 1 of `env.txt` holds the list `steps=A1 A2 A3 A4`. The comment says that the script run_partA.sh ran the steps in this order.
- The `assert` stops the script unless three things hold. A3 directly follows A2 in that list. The first header line of `A3.csv` is line 1 of the file. The last process of `A2.csv` was launched before the first process of `A3.csv`.
- Then `a3_prev` is the last process of `A2.csv`, and `a3_first` is the first process of `A3.csv`.
- `write_json` names `a3_prev` in the description of the field `kernel_before` (lines 931 to 936).

Finds the hardware error records during the baselines A-2 and A-3.
- `a2_records`: every record whose time lies in `a2_window`, both ends included. Each one also gets `proc`, the last process of `A1.csv` that was launched at or before the time of the record, and `next`, the process after it. This data has 4 such records.
- `i3`: the places of the processes of `A3.csv` whose tag is `onebuf-ms500-1`, `onebuf-ms500-2` or `onebuf-ms500-3`. These three processes are baseline A-3.
- `a3_window`: from the launch of the first of them to the launch of the process after the last of them.
- `a3_records`: the records inside `a3_window` (none in this data).
- `n_records_boot`: the number of all records of the journal.

`journal_release` is the Linux kernel release of that boot, from the text `Linux version ...` in line 1 of the journal. `facts_text.py` stops the script unless it equals the release of the rerun. `out['pre']` holds machine settings that were saved in the same boot, in the folder `R/fwtest-20261117/pre`:
- `when`: the time of the save, from `when.txt` (2026-11-17 03:43:42 UTC).
- `cmdline`: the Linux boot arguments, from `cmdline.txt`. `facts_text.py` stops the script unless they equal the boot arguments in the `== cmdline` line of the go.sh log.
- `gov`: the two lines of `gov.txt`. In this file they read `128 performance` and `2800000`. `facts_text.py` stops the script unless line 1 is `128`, a space and the governor name of the go.sh log, and line 2 is the value `scaling_cur_freq` of CPU 0 of that log.
- A governor is the Linux policy that sets the CPU frequency. `scaling_cur_freq` is a file of Linux that gives the current frequency of a CPU in kHz (Linux kernel documentation, page "CPU Performance Scaling"). So the value 2800000 of the go.sh log is 2.8 GHz. The same page says that in most cases the value is the frequency that Linux last requested from the hardware. It also says that the CPU may run at another frequency.
- `thp`: the huge-page setting of Linux, from `thp.txt` (`[always] madvise never` in this file). `facts_text.py` stops the script unless it equals the `enabled` value in the `== thp` line of the go.sh log.

- `k5_last_line` is the number of lines of the Linux kernel log `k-5.txt`. `k5_last` is the time stamp of its last line (`Nov 17 03:44:00` in this file).
- `q_speed` is the memory speed of the entry `DIMM Frequency` in `questions.json` of the folder `R/uefisettings-20261117`, the saved list of firmware settings. It is 8000 MT/s in this file.
- The function returns `out`.

`main` calls this function after `collect` (line 1036). It appends 27 checks to the list `D['checks']` in a fixed order. It changes no record.
- `yn` turns a truth value into the text `yes` or `NO`.
- `chk` appends one check: a key, the pass flag `ok` and one line of text.
- `per` builds a text with one value per rerun folder, for example `T72L1 10, T72L2 10`.
- A check that fails does not stop this function. The stop comes later: `render` ends the script when a check failed (see `main`, line 1037).
- A failed `assert` (lines 807 and 858) ends the script immediately.
segments.heading: Function `run_checks`: 27 integrity checks

segments.text: Checks `log-go` and `log-go2`, one per driver log. A check passes when the log holds a line `ALLDONE` and no line that starts with `FAILED`. The text says whether the last line is `ALLDONE`, and it gives the number of `FAILED` lines.
segments.heading: Checks 1 to 5: logs, boot id, MemTotal, logins

segments.text:
Checks `boot` and `memtotal`.
- `states`: the state lines of both logs (18 in this data).
- `boot` passes when the boot ids of all state lines and of the 3 `probe.txt` files of part A are one value, and this value is the boot id in `try6.txt`.
- `memtotal` passes in the same way for MemTotal. Each `probe.txt` gives two values: one from the start and one from the end of its session.
- `try6.txt` is the record of 12 modules at 7200 MT/s. So the two checks show that every step of the rerun ran in the boot of that record, with the same MemTotal.

Check `logins`. It passes when three things hold:
- Every state line shows 0 logins and the marker `absent`.
- Every `probe.txt` of part A shows 0 logins.
- The launch line of every bwx12 folder shows 0 logins.
The text gives the counts, for example `18 of 18 state lines`.

Checks `A-shape` and `A-order`, on the 3 `threads120.csv` files of part A.
- `order13`: binary, kernel and round of the 24 processes of baseline A-1, in file order.
- `shape` returns three values of one file: the number of processes, the distinct numbers of interval rows per process, and the distinct values of the column `threads` of the interval rows.
- `A-shape` passes when every file has 24 processes with 3 interval rows each, the column `threads` is 120 in every row, and the column `rep` of each process reads 0, 1, 2.
- `A-order` passes when the processes of every file have the same order of binary, kernel and round as in A-1.
- With both checks passed, each session holds 2 processes x 3 interval rows of `bw_old` with the kernel `read`, and the same of `bw_new`. That gives 18 interval rows per read kernel in the 3 sessions.
segments.heading: Checks 6 and 7: shape and order of part A

segments.text:
Three checks on the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun (`X`).
- `I-rows`: the number of I rows of the csv must equal the expected number, and it must equal the number of intervals that `fd.bwx_intervals` built from the T rows. The expected number is 10 for parts L and I (2 rounds x 5 kernels) and 6 for part C (2 rounds x 3 kernels).
- `rc`: `launches.txt` must hold exactly one launch line, and its exit status must be `0`.
- `stderr`: `stderr.txt` must hold 0 bytes.
segments.heading: Checks 8 to 13: rows of the bwx12 files of the rerun

segments.text:
Checks `6456` and `flags`, on the T rows of the 9 files.
- `6456` passes when every interval has 120 T rows and passes the 64+56 test: 64 threads on CPUs 0-63 and 56 threads on CPUs 64-119, on 120 different CPUs.
- `D['n_T_rows']`: the number of T rows of all intervals (8880 in this data, which is 74 intervals x 120 threads).
- `vals`: the distinct values of the flags column over these T rows.
- `flags` passes when `-` is the only value. The text also gives the number of flagged rows per folder.
- Neither check removes a row. A T row with a flag stays in the sum of its interval.

Check `P-rows`, on the page state of the buffers. A P row is stored as a tuple of the values after the leading `P`. Counted from 0, its places 4, 5 and 7 hold the columns `kB_total`, `kB_huge` and `thp_fault_fallback`.
- `huge(x)`: the number of P rows of a folder in which `kB_huge` equals `kB_total`. In such a row the whole buffer is on huge pages.
- `tot`: the distinct values of `kB_total`. The only value in this data is 262144 kB. With 1 kB = 1024 bytes this is 256 MiB (1 MiB = 2^20 bytes), the size of one buffer. The list is kept as `D['P_kB']` for the text of FACTS.md.
- `fb`: the distinct values of `thp_fault_fallback`. The text prints them. They are not part of the pass condition.
- The check passes when every folder has at least one P row and `kB_huge` equals `kB_total` in all of its P rows.

**The rate of this script against the rate that bwx12 printed.**
- `iv['total']` is the rate that the records use: the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9. The bytes of each thread are divided by the elapsed time of that thread.
- `iv['I_agg']` is the column `aggregate_GBps` of the I row of the same interval. bwx12 computed it as the bytes of all threads / the longest per-thread time, and it printed 2 decimal places.
- `dmax(x)`: the largest absolute difference of the two values over the intervals of one folder, in GB/s.
- The check passes when the largest `dmax` of the 9 folders is below `agg_limit` = 0.05 GB/s. This limit is a choice of the script.
- In this data the largest difference is 0.018 GB/s, in T72L1 [Ref9].
- Example: the interval of round 0, position 0 (oldread) of T72L1 has `total` = 462.300 GB/s and `I_agg` = 462.29 GB/s [Ref8].
segments.heading: Check 14, `I-agg`: sum of the T rows against the I row

segments.text:
Checks `args` and `args-R8`, on the arguments of the bwx12 processes.
- `spec`: the content of `like.spec`, `cfwd.spec` and `crev.spec`, each split at the first `|` into tag and arguments.
- `args` passes when the tag and the arguments of the launch line of every rerun folder equal the spec file of that folder. The arguments hold the stop rule (`--stop common`), the interval length (`--min-ms 6000`) and the kernel sequence (`--seq`).
- With the common stop, bwx12 sets one deadline for all threads, 6000 ms after the common start time. A thread stops at its first clock reading at or after the deadline. So 6000 ms is not a lower limit for the timed span of one thread. In the 8880 T rows of the rerun the column `elapsed_s` lies between 5.999979 s and 6.000457 s.
- `args-R8` passes when the arguments of `like.spec` equal the arguments of the `a6456` launch line of L-1 and of F72d12.
- With both checks passed, part L, control I, baseline L-1 and F72d12 ran with the same argument line.
segments.heading: Checks 15 to 22: arguments, checksums, Linux release, runnable tasks

segments.text:
Checks `sha-bw` and `sha-ra`. `p13` is the result of `open_probe13`.
- `ok`: the sha256 values of `bw_old` and `bw_new` in the 3 `probe.txt` files of part A equal the values in `probe.txt` of 2026-11-13. ra.sh computed the values of part A on CRB with `sha256sum`, once at the start of each session [Ref10]. Before that, ra.sh tests both binaries against the two sha256 values that are written in its own text, and it stops when the test fails.
- `ok2`: `env.txt` of the folder `partA-20261113T205055Z` holds the same two values. This folder holds the baselines A-2 and A-3.
- `sha-bw` passes when `ok` and `ok2` are true. Then part A of the rerun and the baselines A-1, A-2 and A-3 ran the same two binaries.
- `sha-ra` passes when the sha256 of the local file `S/ra.sh` equals the value of `ra.sh` in each `probe.txt`. ra.sh wrote that value on CRB from its own file.
- The script computes no sha256 of a binary. The files `bw_old`, `bw_new` and `bwx12` are not in the local folders. So `sha-bw` and `sha-bwx12` (next row) compare only sha256 values that the records hold.

Check `sha-bwx12`.
- `shas`: the distinct sha256 values of bwx12 in `env.txt` of the 9 rerun folders.
- rx.sh does not compute this value. It takes the value from its third argument. It tests the binary against the value with `sha256sum -c` and stops when the test fails. Then it writes the value into `env.txt`. go.sh and go2.sh pass their value `SHA` as this argument.
- `same12`: the earlier bwx12 data sets, out of 9 names, whose `env.txt` holds a value of `shas`.
- `go_sha`: the value of the line `SHA=` in the local `go.sh`. go.sh tests the bwx12 binary on CRB against this value.
- The check passes when `shas` holds one value, all 9 earlier data sets hold it, and it equals `go_sha`. Then parts L and C, control I and these 9 data sets ran the same bwx12 binary.

Check `sha-local`.
- The files `local.sha` and `go2.sha` in `S` hold one line per file: a sha256 value and a file name. `listed` maps each file name to its value.
- This data lists 6 files: `go.sh`, `go2.sh`, `ra.sh` and the 3 spec files.
- `bad` holds the names whose local file in `S` has another sha256. The check passes when `bad` is empty.
- The check reads local files only. A pass shows that the 6 files in `S` have not changed since the two lists were written. The row of lines 853 to 866 says what is known about the copies on CRB.
- The stored sheet shows a pass. A new build fails since 2026-11-24. Line 20 of go.sh was edited on that day (the text of one message). So `bad` holds `go.sh`. With the old line 20 put back the check passes again [Ref17].

Check `uname`.
- `rel_`: the distinct values of the Linux kernel release in the 3 `probe.txt` files and the 9 `env.txt` files.
- `cmd_rel`: the text after `vmlinuz-` in the `== cmdline` line of the go.sh log. In this log the boot arguments start with `BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinuz-7.1.3-arm-agi-20260916-v0.7.2-g4dbc8bb88858`. So `cmd_rel` is the release part of the name of the Linux image.
- The check passes when `rel_` holds one value and this value equals `cmd_rel`.

Check `runnable`, on the runnable tasks before a launch.
- `rx_`: the number of runnable tasks in the launch line of each of the 9 bwx12 folders. `ra_`: the value `runnable=` of each of the 3 `probe.txt` files.
- `limit`: the number in the text `$r -le 2` of `ra.sh`, read from the script. ra.sh waits before its first process until at most 2 tasks are runnable.
- `sleep_`: the number in the first line of `ra.sh` that starts with `sleep` (5 s).
- The check passes when the largest of the 12 values is not above `limit`. In this data the value is 1 in the 9 launch lines and 2 in the 3 `probe.txt` files.
- The text of the check also says what the data do not show. ra.sh reads the value, then sleeps 5 s, then writes the probe line. So the number of runnable tasks at the first launch of part A is not recorded.

**Check x-k120: a second reader of the part A rows.** stat_k120.py reads the interval rows a second time with its own parser [Ref5].
- `pairs`: the 3 part A folders of the rerun, the folder of A-1, and two folders under `S/base8000`. These two hold copies of the A-2 and A-3 processes in the form of `threads120.csv`. The records of A-2 and A-3 come from the raw `A1.csv` and `A3.csv`.
- The two readers must return the same number of processes per folder, or the `assert` stops the script.
- For every interval row the check compares four values: `aggregate_GBps` (column 7), `per_thread_min_GBps` (column 8), `per_thread_max_GBps` (column 9), and the pass count (column 5 / column 3, rounded down). It also compares binary and kernel of each process.
- The comparison is exact equality. No difference is allowed.
- `n_k` counts the compared interval rows (333 in this data). `bad_k` counts the processes with any difference. The check passes when `bad_k` is 0.
- Line 805 adds each `threads120.csv` to `fd.OPENED`. The reason: stat_k120.py does not open it through `fd._open`.
segments.heading: Checks 23 and 24: the rates against two other readers

segments.text:
**Check x-bwx: a second reader of the bwx rows.** stat_bwx.py computes the rate of every interval with its own parser [Ref6].
- `folders`: the 9 rerun folders and the 11 folders of the earlier bwx12 and bwx11 data sets (`D['rx']`). The folders of the first runner bwx (`D['step']`) are not part of this check.
- Every interval of the csv files that this script read from these 20 folders is looked up in the rows of stat_bwx.py by file name, round, position and kernel. This includes the intervals that the filter `POS01` kept out of the records. An interval that stat_bwx.py does not return ends the script with the Python error `KeyError` (line 823).
- An interval counts as different when the total, the sum of mesh 0 or the sum of mesh 1 differs by more than 1e-9 GB/s (1 byte per second). It also counts when the 64+56 test or the number of flagged rows differs.
- The two scripts add the per-thread rates in a different order. So a limit above 0 is needed. stat_bwx.py adds all T rows in file order. This script adds each mesh first and then the two sums. The largest difference in this data is about 5e-13 GB/s.
- `n_x` counts the compared intervals (297 in this data: 74 of the rerun and 223 earlier ones). The check passes when `bad_x` is 0.

Check `earlier`, on the bwx records that do not belong to the rerun.
- `b`: the records that have a 64+56 value and whose data set is not `rerun-L`, `rerun-C` or `control-I`. Only bwx records have this value. This data has 386 such records.
- `okb`: the number of them that pass the 64+56 test and have 0 flagged T rows.
- `errs`: the bytes of `stderr.txt` of the 11 folders of `D['rx']`, added. `rcs`: the distinct exit statuses of the 17 processes whose csv files this script reads. The `launches.txt` files of these folders hold 52 launch lines. The exit statuses of the other 35 processes are not tested here.
- The check passes when `okb` equals the size of `b`, `errs` is 0, and `0` is the only exit status.
- The exit status and `stderr.txt` of the folders of the first runner bwx are not tested here.
segments.heading: Checks 25 to 27: earlier data, rx.sh, arguments of part A

segments.text:
Check `sha-rx`, on the runner script rx.sh. The comment says that it was added after the checks above. Their numbers then stay as they were.
- `rx`: the sha256 of the local `rx.sh`. `rxsha`: the value of the line `RXSHA=` in the local `go.sh` and `go2.sh`.
- `has_stop`: both scripts hold the line that tests `rx.sh` against `RXSHA` with `sha256sum` and calls `fail` when the test fails. In both scripts `fail` prints a line that starts with `FAILED:`, prints a state line and ends the script with the exit status 1. `has_stop` also requires that both scripts hold the first part of that function, the `echo` of the `FAILED:` line. It does not test the rest of the function.
- `n_failed`: the number of `FAILED` lines in the two logs.

- `crb_texts`: the text of the 2 logs, of the 3 `probe.txt` files and of the 9 `env.txt` files of the rerun. `local_sha`: the sha256 values of the local rx.sh, go.sh and go2.sh. Since 2026-11-24 the value for go.sh is that of the edited file. It is not the value of the text that ran.
- The `assert` in line 858 stops the script when one of these texts holds one of the three checksums.
- The comment in line 853 names the limit of the check: no record of the rerun holds a checksum of rx.sh, go.sh or go2.sh that was taken on CRB. So the check uses the local copies of go.sh and go2.sh. The text of the check says this.
- The record of the Claude Code session of 2026-11-17 holds a test of both driver scripts on CRB [Ref14]. This record lies outside the project folder, and this script does not read it. Two commands of that record wrote `local.sha` and `go2.sha` in the local folder `S` and copied the listed files to CRB. There they ran `sha256sum -c`, which compares each file with its sha256 in the list. The output shows `go.sh: OK` and `go2.sh: OK`.
- The check passes when both `RXSHA` values equal `rx`, `has_stop` is true and `n_failed` is 0. Then neither driver script stopped at its test of rx.sh on CRB.
- The text names the check `sha-local` by its number. Line 866 takes the number from the place of that check in the list.

Check `A-args`, on the arguments of part A. It compares part A of the rerun with baseline A-1, the first test of 2026-11-13.
- `hdr(p)`: six values of the `-- binary` header line of a process: binary, kernel, threads, cpus, bytes and round.
- `n_same`: the number of rerun processes whose six values equal those of the process at the same place in A-1. `n_all`: the number of all rerun processes.
- `hv`: the distinct values of threads, cpus and bytes over the processes of all 4 files. `bw`: the distinct ends of the `# bandwidth:` line that the binary prints. This end holds threads, bytes per thread, `min_ms` and `thp`.
- `same_fn`: the 5 lines of the function `one` in `ra.sh` equal the 5 lines of `one` in `run_kernels.sh`. `one` starts one benchmark process.
- `has_opts`: the line of `one` that starts the binary ends with `--reps 3 --min-ms 500 >> "$1"`. So each process times 3 intervals of at least 500 ms each.
- `rk_ok`: the sha256 of the local `run_kernels.sh` equals the value in `probe.txt` of 2026-11-13.

The check passes when all of these hold: `n_same` equals `n_all`, `hv` holds one value, `bw` holds one value that is not empty, and `same_fn`, `has_opts` and `rk_ok` are true. In this data all 72 header lines of the rerun equal those of A-1, with threads 120, cpus 0-119 and bytes 256M. The binary printed `min_ms=500 thp=madvise` in all 96 processes of the 4 files [Ref9]. The function then returns the list of checks.

`main` calls this function with `D`, the verdicts `V` and the path `S/facts.json` (line 1038).
- Lines 902 to 1014 build the dictionary `meta`, the first of the three parts of the file.
- `meta` describes the run. It holds no interval record.
- Its first entries are a title, the names of the scripts that wrote the file, and the folder paths `R` and `S`.
segments.heading: Function `write_json`: writes facts.json

segments.text:
`units` and `rate_kinds`: texts that explain fields of the records.
- `GBps`: GB/s with GB = 1e9 bytes.
- `load1_at_launch`, `gap_s`, `passes`, `min_ms`, `speed_MTps`: one text each. The text of `passes` holds the number of records of the kernels `copy` and `asmcopy` (96 in this data), counted with `fd.sel`.
- `rate_kinds` repeats the two rate formulas. `fd.KIND_A` is the formula of part A: the column `aggregate_GBps` of the csv. The text adds how the binary computed this column: the sum of the bytes of all threads / the longest per-thread time [Ref13]. `fd.KIND_X` is the formula of the bwx runners: the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9.
- The text of the bwx formula adds that facts.json rounds this rate to 0.001 GB/s, and that FACTS.md formats the value that is not rounded.

`fields`: 15 texts for the reader of facts.json.
- 14 texts explain one field of a record each. The text `q2_rows` explains the keys of a row in `verdicts.q2_rows`.
- Only the text of `kernel_before` holds values from the data. It names the process that ran directly before the first process of baseline A-3 (`a3_prev` of `open_probe13`).
- Three texts concern rate fields. `mesh0_GBps` is the sum over the threads on CPUs 0-63. `mesh1_GBps` is the sum over the threads on CPUs 64-127.
- Both fields hold a value in bwx records only. In a part A record they are `null`.
- `per_thread_avg_GBps` holds a value in part A records only. It is the csv column of the same name, which the binary rounds to 0.01 GB/s.

More entries of `meta`:
- `rerun`: boot id, module count, memory speed and MemTotal from `try6.txt`. `speed_proof` names the line of `try6.txt` that holds the memory speed, and it says that the speed was not read during the rerun. The entry also holds the times of the first and the last state line of go.sh and of go2.sh. Two fixed values say that the Linux kernel log was not read and that root rights were not used.
- `launches`: the 12 steps of the rerun in time order. Each has tag, part, session, three times, `gap_s`, the 1-minute load average at the first launch and the start state.
- `checks`: the 27 checks with key, pass flag and text.
- `counts`: the number of all records and the number per data set, in the order in which the data sets first appear. Records are counted here. No rate is added.
- `rules` and `control_note`: two fixed texts.

`F72d12_boot`: the reason why the records of F72d12 carry the boot of the rerun. The folder of F72d12 holds no boot id.
- The entry gives the launch time and the end time of its process.
- It gives two readings of the same boot id: `try6.txt` before the process and the first state line of the go.sh log after it.
- It also gives row 0 of `boots.txt` and of `gaps.txt` with their times.

`hardware_error_records`: a copy of what `hw_records` and `hw_compare` built (`D['hw']`, `D['hw_cmp']`).
- `processes`: one entry per process of L-1 to L-4, R0 and R0b, with the hardware error records of the journal inside its process window.
- A record of the kind `inside` or `possible` carries its interval. Lines 994 to 996 round the start time and the end time of that interval to 0.001 s and its rate to 0.001 GB/s. The rate is `total`, the sum over the T rows.
- `F72d12`: the value `hwerr` of row 0 of `gaps.txt`. `rerun`: a fixed text that says that the Linux kernel log was not read for the rerun.
- `all_intervals`: the result of `hw_compare_json` (line 400).

`firmware_settings`: a copy of what `open_fw` read. It holds the saved settings lists with file name and file time, the replies of the `set` calls of the firmware settings tool, and the last reading of the memory speed setting. A fixed note says that no settings list was saved in the boot of the rerun.

The file is first written under the name `facts.json.tmp`. `r3all` goes through nested dictionaries and lists and rounds every float (a floating-point number) to 3 decimal places with `r3` (line 38). It returns every other value unchanged.

- Line 1025 writes `meta` as it was built, then the verdicts after `r3all`. `meta` does not go through `r3all`.
- Line 1027: `rounded` returns a copy of a record in which every float is rounded to 3 decimal places with the Python function `round`. For a rate this is 0.001 GB/s.
- The float fields of a record are `GBps`, `mesh0_GBps`, `mesh1_GBps`, `per_thread_min_GBps`, `per_thread_max_GBps`, `per_thread_avg_GBps`, `load1_at_launch` and `gap_s`.
- A part A rate has 2 decimal places in the csv. The rounding does not change it. A bwx rate changes. Example: the sum 462.30001702 GB/s of T72L1 is written as 462.3.
- Line 1028 writes one line per record, in the order of `D['recs']`. The records in memory keep their values.
- `os.replace` then renames the file to `facts.json`. So a reader never sees a part of the file.
segments.heading: Rounding of the rates in facts.json

segments.text:
The entry point of the script. `facts_text.py` is imported here, inside the function.
- `collect` reads the result files and builds the records in `D`. `run_checks` appends the 27 checks.
- `facts_text.render` computes the statistics from the field `GBps` of the records. It returns the verdicts `V` and the text of FACTS.md [Ref2]. The lowest, the median and the highest rate of each kernel and the percent values are computed there, not in this file.
- **A failed check stops the script inside this call.** `render` calls `section4` of `facts_text4.py`. That function ends the script with an error message unless every check has `ok` true. Then no output file is written, and the exit status is 1.
- A test that wrote no file confirmed this. With one check set to failed, `render` ended the script with the message `facts_text.py: the data do not show the pattern of a sentence: all integrity checks pass`.
- `write_json` writes `S/facts.json`.
- The text is written to `S/FACTS.md.tmp`. Then the file is renamed to `S/FACTS.md`.
segments.heading: Function `main`: collect, check, render, write

segments.text:
- With the argument `--print` the script prints the text of FACTS.md.
- `bad` is the list of the checks with `ok` false. The script prints the number of checks and the number of failed checks, then one line `FAILED` with key and text per failed check.
- It prints the number of records and the verdicts `Q1` and `Q2`.
- Line 1052 gives the exit status 1 when `bad` is not empty.
- In the present code these lines are reached only when all checks passed. The reason: `render` stops the script before them when a check failed (see the row above). So `bad` is empty here, no `FAILED` line is printed, and the script ends with the exit status 0.
When the file is run as a script, Python calls `main`.
